steps: Unpack & inspect
Check the stove and parts for damage; remove packing from the flue collar and above the baffle. Keep the safety label secured in its clip behind the ash lip.

Pack list: owner's manual, three boxes of refractory stone, optional 90-degree Romex connector, side stone retainer brackets, 2 leg leveling bolts. Report damaged or missing parts to your Hearthstone dealer immediately.

Remove the packaging material in the flue collar and above the baffle before installing the chimney. The safety label is attached by a cable in the bottom of the stove, behind the ash lip assembly: don't damage it when fitting or removing the blower, and secure it in its clip before reinstalling the ash lip.

The manual's diagrams show typical installations and are specific to the Simpson Dura-Vent brand.
Valence bracket & leveling bolts
Fit the rear valence cover bracket over the opening in the top of the stove before installing. Thread the 2 leg leveling bolts into the welded nuts on each side to set height.
Clearances & floor protection
Confirm stove and liner clearances to walls, floor, ceiling and chimney chase. Combustible floor: non-combustible protector at least 41-1/2" x 16" (US) or 48" x 18" (Canada).
Outside air (optional)
Kit #94-53500 to a minimum 3" duct, terminating no higher than the stove's air intake, screened with ¼" x ¼" mesh. In Canada, fasten the stove to the floor.
Chimney, liner & block-off
Listed 6" stainless flexible connector to a listed 6" stainless liner the full height of the chimney; seal the damper area with a block-off plate. Never share the flue.

Connect the insert to a listed 6" stainless steel flexible connector feeding a listed 6" stainless steel liner that runs continuously to the top of the chimney (class 3 of ULC-S635 or ULC-S640, or UL1777). Seal the damper area with a sealed block-off plate or a plug of noncombustible material such as unfaced fiberglass insulation. Remove the damper or lock it open.

Prefabricated metal fireplace

  • Listed per UL 127 or ULC S610, with a full-height listed chimney liner (ULC-S635 or ULC-S640).
  • Room air must be kept out of the chimney cavity; louvers and cooling-air ports must not be blocked; no blocked circulating chambers.
  • No alterations, except removable external trim (stored on or in the fireplace) and removing the damper to fit the liner.
  • Provide a means of removing the insert to clean the flue, and rivet the supplied permanent metal warning label to the fireplace's outside wall.

Masonry chimney

  • Have a professional examine it for cracks, loose mortar, deterioration and blockage; complete repairs first.
  • Mortared brick or modular block at least 4" thick, or rubble or stone: liner required. Tile liner: 5/8" minimum wall, refractory mortar, at least 1" air space.
  • The cleanout door must close completely and seal tightly.

Height

At least 3 feet above the roof opening, and 2 feet above any part of the roof within 10 feet horizontally. Recommended minimum 10 feet off the floor; recommended maximum 30 feet.

Not approved for mobile home installation. Never connect to a flue used by another appliance or to any air distribution duct or system.
Connect to the flue collar
Crimped ends toward the stove; secure every joint with three sheet metal screws, using #10 x 1/2" screws in the flue collar's pre-drilled holes.
Check the draft
Required draft is 0.06" to 0.1" WC; check it at installation. Above 0.1" WC, install a stovepipe damper.
Blower hardwire (optional)
Remove the circular knockout in the rear of the stove body and thread on the supplied 90-degree Romex to hardwire the blower.
Install the refractory stones
Rear stones (1-0400-601) first, then side-rear (1-0400-602) and side-front (1-0400-603) on each side; secure with the side stone retaining brackets.

The three boxes hold two rear stones (1-0400-601), two side-rear stones (1-0400-602) and two side-front stones (1-0400-603). If the side stone retaining brackets (5460-021 and 5460-022) are installed, loosen the screw and slide each bracket toward the front to remove it.

  1. Place the two rear stones in the back of the stove first.
  2. On each side, slide in the rear side stone, then the front side stone.
  3. Reinstall the side stone retaining brackets to secure them.

panels.title: Stove smokes
items: Operating technique → fully open the primary air control one minute before opening the door
Cold chimney or reverse draft → preheat the chimney; briefly open a window in the room
Blocked chimney → check chimney and stovepipe for blockage or creosote
Oversized chimney → reline to the appropriate diameter; chimney too short → lengthen it
Air infiltration into the chimney → seal connections and openings; check clean-out doors
More than one appliance on the flue → disconnect the others and seal openings

panels.title: Back-puffing or gas explosions
items: Operating technique → open the primary air fully one minute before opening the door; keep it open a few minutes after reloading
Extra low burn rate → burn at a higher rate
Chimney down-draft → install a chimney cap
Excessive ash build-up → empty ashes more often; avoid poor quality or green wood

panels.title: Uncontrolled or short burn
items: Unsealed or open door → close it tightly or replace the gaskets; air leaking at the glass gasket → replace it
Excessive draft → operate at low burn; draft over 0.1 wc needs stovepipe damper(s)
Extra long chimney → shorten it or install stovepipe damper(s)
Oversized chimney → reline to the proper diameter
High winds or hilltop location → install a chimney cap

panels.title: Insufficient heat
items: Poor quality, low Btu or green wood → air-dried wood, preferably dried at least one year
Low burn rate → operate at a higher burn rate
Cold exterior chimney → reline or insulate it
Leaky stovepipe or chimney → check the installation
Too much heat loss from the house → insulate, upgrade or caulk windows, seal openings

fire.title: Starting a fire
fire.html:
Once the insert is broken in, this is the everyday way to start it.

  1. Open the front door: pull up on the wood handle and swing the door open.
  2. Place five or six double sheets of tightly twisted newspaper in the center of the firebox. Arrange about 10 pieces of kindling, 1/2" in diameter and 10" to 16" long, in a tee-pee over the paper. No grate: the fire sits on the firebox floor.
  3. Fully open the air control by pulling the lever all the way left.
  4. Light the paper. Leave the door slightly open until the kindling catches and the chimney starts to draw.
  5. Close the door. Once the kindling is burning, add logs, small ones first, keeping them away from the glass.
  6. Set the burn rate with the air control: left for more heat, right for less.

To latch the door, push it tight toward the firebox, then push the handle in and down until it latches. Tug gently to check.

Reloading

Open the air control fully one minute before you open the door. Open the door a crack, pause, then open it fully so smoke clears first. Reload on a bed of hot, red coals. If the fire has burned down to charcoal, run it at a medium to high rate for about 10 minutes.

Never use gasoline, kerosene, charcoal lighter fluid or similar liquids to start or freshen a fire. Keep the door closed while it burns.

breakin.title: Breaking in your insert
breakin.html:
The soapstone has to be seasoned: its natural moisture must be driven out slowly, and the furnace cement must cure. Over-firing a new stove can crack the soapstone. Build your first fires, and the first fire of each season, this way:

  1. Place five or six double sheets of tightly twisted newspaper in the center of the firebox, with about ten pieces of kindling (1/2" diameter, 10" to 16" long) in a crisscross over it.
  2. Fully open the primary air control and light the paper. Leave the door slightly open until the kindling catches, then close it.
  3. Aim for a steady, low fire that makes the stove warm but not hot to the touch. Steam, boiling moisture or hissing means the soapstone is too hot. Add a few small chunks of wood at most.
  4. Once the stove is warm but not hot, close the primary air control, let the fire die out, and let the stove return to room temperature.

Smoke and smells at first

Early fires give off some smoke and fumes as paints and oils cure. Open a few windows; it usually fades after 10 to 20 minutes. Break-in fires run cool and can build creosote fast, so inspect the stovepipe and chimney once break-in is done.

Note: the break-in steps on p. 21 say to pull the handle towards you to open the air and push it inward to close it; pp. 18 and 22 say left for more air, right for less.

air.title: Burn rates & over-firing
air.html:
The primary air control lever sits under the ash lip. More air means a faster, hotter fire; less air means a slower burn and less heat. It never closes completely.

LowLever all the way right
Medium-lowFrom low, pull left a little less than 1/2"
Medium-highFrom low, pull left a little less than 1"
HighLever all the way left

Medium-low is the typical setting, and the one to use if you'll leave the insert unattended. Long periods on low build creosote, so inspect the venting often if you burn low a lot. The minimum burn rate is set at the factory, and federal regulations forbid altering it.

Signs of over-firing

Never over-fire your stove. Over-firing means running hotter than a normal high burn. It damages the stove, and that damage isn't covered by the warranty. Watch for warped parts, short burn times, a roaring sound in the stove or stovepipe, or a discolored stovepipe.

Causes are too much draft (your dealer can take a draft reading), the wrong fuel, or worn gaskets and doors left open. If you suspect over-firing, stop using the insert and call your dealer.

glass.title: Cleaning the glass
glass.html:
The door glass is a tough ceramic that can handle up to 2300° F. Clean it only when the fire is out and the glass is cool.

  1. Inside: rub with a damp paper towel dipped in gray ash, in a circular motion.
  2. When the deposits are gone, finish inside and out with window cleaner or a commercial stove glass cleaner, following its instructions.
  3. Wipe off with a soft cloth or black and white newsprint.

Never use a razor blade, steel wool or anything abrasive: scratches weaken the glass. If the glass always stays dirty, the fire is too cool or the wood is wet, and creosote builds faster.

Broken or chipped glass

Don't run the insert with broken glass. Replace it right away with the ceramic glass made for this stove, from your dealer. Never strike or slam the door.

Glass kit94-58605
The manual also prints the glass kit as PN: 96-58605 (p. 24); p. 23 and the parts list on p. 38 give 94-58605.
Note: p. 24 suggests window cleaner or a commercial stove glass cleaner, then says to use only a cleaner made specifically for woodstoves.
Note: p. 23 says only a qualified service person should replace the glass; p. 24 says to wear work gloves and safety glasses if you do it yourself.

wood.title: What wood to burn
wood.html:
Burn only natural, untreated firewood (cordwood). The insert isn't designed for any other fuel.

  • Season it. Green wood burns poorly. Split, stack and air-dry it for one year. Seasoned wood is typically at or near 20% moisture; a hand-held moisture meter will tell you.
  • Hardwood or softwood. Softwoods burn hotter and faster; hardwoods burn longer and make better coals. Air-dried seasoned hardwood generally gives higher efficiency and lower emissions.
  • Stack it well. Keep it off the ground on skids or blocks and cover only the top; tarps over the sides trap moisture. Don't store firewood within the stove's clearances.
  • Size it. Logs can be up to 20" long. Never load ice-encrusted wood into a burning stove.

Never burn

Coal, charcoal, pellets, artificial or wax logs, compressed wood, kiln-dried, painted, treated or pressure-treated wood, unseasoned (green or wet) wood, plywood, particleboard, garbage or trash, lawn clippings, materials containing rubber (including tires), materials containing plastic, waste petroleum products, paints or paint thinners, solvents, asphalt products, materials containing asbestos, construction or demolition debris, railroad ties, manure or animal remains, paper products (including colored or glossy paper), cardboard, driftwood (including salt water driftwood) or other previously salt-water saturated materials, highly volatile fuels or combustibles, or flammable fluids.

Burning these can release toxic fumes, or make the insert ineffective and cause smoke. The ban doesn't cover fire starters made from paper, cardboard, sawdust, wax or similar substances, used to start a fire.

Using an unauthorized fuel such as coal could produce high levels of carbon dioxide in the living space. At high levels, carbon dioxide could result in personal injury or death.

The manual's table ranks common species by heat value, from Osage orange and shagbark hickory at the top to white cedar at the bottom.

ash.title: Emptying the ashes
ash.html:
Let the fire die down or go out first. You can leave a thin layer of ash in the firebox.

  1. Push large live coals to the side and remove only the finer ash with a fireplace shovel.
  2. Put the ashes straight into a metal container with a tight-fitting lid. Put nothing else in it, and don't pour water in.
  3. Take the closed container outside right away. Set it on a noncombustible floor or the ground, well away from anything that can burn, liquid fuels and vehicles.
  4. Keep the ashes in the closed container until all the coals are thoroughly cool. Coals in ash can stay hot for several days.

Don't let ash build up around the door opening: it can spill out or pack into the gasket channel and stop the door sealing. The best time is after an overnight fire, when the insert is fairly cool but the chimney still draws the dust up.

Never use wooden or plastic containers, paper or plastic bags, or a trash can with other trash. Never set the container on a combustible surface or vinyl flooring.
How often: empty the ashes at the end of every week, or sooner if the firebox is full (p. 6). When you heat full-time, empty them every two or three days (p. 24).

chimney.title: Chimney & seasonal care
chimney.html:
A slow, cool fire gives off tar and vapors that condense in the chimney as creosote. If it ignites, it burns extremely hot and can damage the chimney or even destroy the house.

Inspect and clean

  • Check the chimney connector and chimney at least once every two months in the heating season, and at least monthly if creosote is building up.
  • Check the top of the chimney, where it's coolest, as well as near the stove.
  • Remove any creosote deposit greater than 1/4". A certified chimney sweep is recommended.
  • Before each heating season, have the whole system professionally inspected, cleaned and repaired if needed.

Prevent it

Burn with the air control fully open for 35 to 45 minutes daily, and for 15 to 20 minutes after each reload.

End of every season

Take apart and clean the chimney connector, replacing rusted pieces. Clean out the inside of the stove. Inspect the door gaskets; replace them every two to three seasons, or sooner if worn.

Dollar bill test (every other month): with the stove cool, shut the door on a dollar bill. If it pulls out with no resistance, adjust the latch or replace the gasket.

blower.title: Using the blower
blower.html:
A blower is already installed behind the faceplate at the bottom of the insert. It moves air around the air jacket to circulate warm air into the room.

The controls are at the lower left of the bottom faceplate: a rocker switch (A) and a rheostat dial (B).

  1. Turn the rheostat clockwise (upward) to switch the blower on.
  2. Pick a mode with the rocker switch, then set the speed with the rheostat.
Auto (switch up)Starts when the insert is warm, stops when it's cold
Manual (switch down)Starts right away; you stop it

To stop it in manual mode, turn the rheostat fully left until it clicks, or change the mode. To turn the blower completely off, turn the rheostat counterclockwise until it stops.

Used regularly, the blower gives a small increase in efficiency. It won't make an undersized insert heat a larger space.

safety.title: Safety & chimney fires
safety.html:
If you have a chimney fire

  1. If the fire is too threatening, leave and call the fire department immediately. If not, do the next three steps.
  2. Close the primary air control.
  3. Close the stovepipe damper, if there is one.
  4. Keep the front door closed.
Never throw water on the stove, stovepipe or chimney. The extreme heat can turn it instantly to steam and cause serious injury.

When it's out, leave the air control closed and let the fire die out completely. Inspect the stove, liner and chimney thoroughly, and fix any damage before you use the insert again.

Every day

  • The insert is hot while it runs. Keep children, pets, clothing and furniture away, and use fireplace gloves.
  • Keep furniture, drapes and other combustibles at least 36" away.
  • Install smoke and CO detectors throughout the home, and keep an "A B C" fire extinguisher handy.
  • Keep the front door closed while it burns. With the optional fire screen in place, never leave the insert unattended.

warranty.title: Warranty at a glance
warranty.html:
Hearthstone's limited warranty covers defects in material or workmanship for the original retail purchaser only, on an insert installed by an authorized Hearthstone dealer or their designated representative. It isn't transferable and starts on the original invoice date.

Stone; cast iron not listed elsewhereLimited Lifetime (10 years)
Door handles and latches; steel components and firebox5 years
Appliance electrical and gas components2 years
Enamel finish, accessories, glass, components not listed elsewhere1 year

Hearthstone pays dealer labor in the first year (dealer-installed units only) and parts shipping in the first 90 days.

Not covered: damage from over-firing, other fuels, or installation, operation or maintenance not per the manual or codes; wear parts such as paint, gaskets, baffles, refractory materials and glass; surface and hairline cracks in stone.

Register at hearthstonestoves.com or mail the form from the document packet; registering isn't required for coverage. For claims, contact your dealer.

Some rows of the grid on p. 40 apply only to certain fuels; check it for refractory, baffles and the air supply system.
Note: the warranty grid on p. 40 lists glass under 1 Year; exclusion 3 on p. 41 lists glass as a wear part that isn't covered.

specOutput.title: Heat output
specOutput.html:
Maximum heat output80,000 BTUs per hour of cordwood max.
EPA test conditions14,200 to 48,200 Btu (output)
Heated areaUp to a maximum of 2,200 square feet

The 80,000 figure is the specification-page maximum (p. 7); the 14,200 to 48,200 range is the output shown under the EPA certification test conditions (p. 2). Insulation, windows, floor plan, stove placement and fuel quality can reduce the area heated. The manual says not to consider the insert the home's primary heat source (p. 4).

specEmis.title: Emissions & efficiency
specEmis.html:
Particulate (EPA 2020, cord wood)1.14 g/hr
Maker's website: EPA Certified 1.22 g/hr.
Weighted efficiency (HHV)68%
Maker's website: Efficiency 64% HHV.
CO, average all burn categories53 g/hr

Tested to EPA Alt 125 where applicable. Efficiency measured and weighted per CSA B415.1-10 across the 4 burn rate categories. The manufacturer-set minimum low burn rate must not be altered (federal regulation).

specFirebox.title: Firebox
specFirebox.html:
Firebox capacity2.5 cubic feet
Maximum log lengthUp To 20"
Burn timeHeatLife Up to 9+ hrs.
Maker's website: HeatLife 8.

Wood per cubic foot of firebox varies from 10 to 25 lbs. depending on species, moisture content and packing density. Burn directly on the firebox floor; no grate. The refractory stones (rear, side-rear, side-front) ship in three boxes and are fitted per Appendix 5; secondary air tubes and baffle per Appendix 4.

Note: the firewood section (p. 19) warns of damage to "the catalysts" and the troubleshooting guide (p. 37) refers to catalysts and a bypass door, but the parts lists (pp. 34-35 and 38) include no catalyst or bypass, and the manual describes secondary air tubes and a baffle (p. 30).
Maker's website: Combustion Non-catalytic.

specFlue.title: Chimney & liner
specFlue.html:
Connector6" diameter stainless steel
LinerListed 6" stainless steel, full length of chimney
Metal chimney6" inside diameter, Type HT (2100° F), UL 103 or ULC S629
Masonry chimney6" inside diameter round, or 8" x 8" square
Existing 8" flueUsable with a reducer
Draft0.06" to 0.1" WC
Chimney heightRecommended 10 feet minimum, 30 feet maximum

Liner must be continuous from the insert to the top of the chimney, class 3 of ULC-S635 or ULC-S640, or UL1777. Chimney size not less than the flue collar, nor more than three times its cross-sectional area; an oversized flue builds creosote. Don't use mild steel, aluminum or galvanized pipe. Above 0.1" WC, install a stovepipe damper; some installations need more than one.

Not approved for mobile home installation. Never connect to a chimney flue used by another appliance.

specFloor.title: Hearth & floor protection
specFloor.html:
US minimum41-1/2" x 16"
Canada minimum48" x 18"
Insulated hearth padNot required; no R-value requirement

Noncombustible protection must be under the stove and extend beyond it, for example a continuous layer of tile, brick, slate, glass or another noncombustible facing. Figure 5 (p. 10) shows the additional floor protection for raised and not-raised installations, with trim and mantel clearances, as a diagram only.

Luxury vinyl plank or tile: some begins to warp at 110° Fahrenheit. Check the flooring maker's limits; extra shielding may be needed.

specClear.title: Clearances to combustibles
specClear.html:
The insert's clearances to walls, trim and mantel appear only as diagrams: Figure 6 (p. 11) and Figure 5 (p. 10). The text gives no values. Dimensions in the figures are from the body of the stove unless otherwise indicated. Check the connector and liner listings for their clearances.

Maker's website: Clearances To combustible mantel (from bottom) 40-3/4″; to side trim (from insert side) 9-1/2″; to side wall (from insert side) 19″. Install to the clearance diagrams in the manual.
Furniture, drapes, other combustiblesAt least 36"
Interior chimneyAt least 2" to combustibles; insulation at least 2" away
Exterior chimneyAt least 1" to combustibles

Fire stops are required where an interior chimney passes through floors or ceilings. Clearances can be reduced with an NFPA-approved wall protection system, with approval of the authority having jurisdiction (NFPA Code 211).

specAir.html:
